paragraphs.text: A coarse-grained model for 1 disordered and multi-domain 2 proteins 3

sections.title: Fan Cao1, Sören von Bülow1, Giulio Tesei1, Kresten Lindorff-Larsen1* 4

paragraphs.text: *For correspondence: lindorff@bio.ku.dk (KL-L) 1Structural Biology and NMR Laboratory & the Linderstrøm-Lang Centre for Protein 5 Science, Department of Biology, University of Copenhagen, Copenhagen, Denmark 6 7

Abstract Many proteins contain more than one folded domain, and such modular multi-domain proteins 8 help expand the functional repertoire of proteins. Because of their larger size and often substantial dynamics, 9 it may be difficult to characterize the conformational ensembles of multi-domain proteins by simulations. 10 Here, we present a coarse-grained model for multi-domain proteins that is both fast and provides an 11 accurate description of the global conformational properties in solution. We show that the accuracy of a 12 one-bead-per-residue coarse-grained model depends on how the interaction sites in the folded domains are 13 represented. Specifically, we find excessive domain-domain interactions if the interaction sites are located at 14 the position of the C훼atoms. We also show that if the interaction sites are located at the centre of mass of the 15 residue, we obtain good agreement between simulations and experiments across a wide range of proteins. 16 We then optimize our previously described CALVADOS model using this centre-of-mass representation, and 17 validate the resulting model using independent data. Finally, we use our revised model to simulate phase 18 separation of both disordered and multi-domain proteins. Our results provide a starting point for 19 understanding interactions between folded and disordered regions in proteins, and how these regions affect 20 the propensity of proteins to self-associate and undergo phase separation. 21 22

Introduction 23 Multi-domain proteins (MDPs) consist of more than one folded domain that are often connected by linkers or 24 longer intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), and make up a large fraction (around 50%) of the proteomes in 25 eukaryotic and prokaryotic organisms (Han et al., 2007; Van Der Lee et al., 2014). Like intrinsically disordered 26 proteins (IDPs), MDPs can display large-amplitude motions that may play prominent roles in biomolecular func- 27 tions like signalling, catalysis and regulation (Mackereth and Sattler, 2012; Van Der Lee et al., 2014; Delaforge 28 et al., 2016; Bondos et al., 2021). 29 The biological functions of MDPs depend both on the properties of the folded domains and the disordered 30 regions, and so characterizing the conformational ensembles can be key to understanding how these proteins 31 function. In many cases, the folded and disordered regions are studied separately, but the folded domains 32 might affect the conformational properties of the disordered regions (Mittal et al., 2018; Taneja and Hole- 33 house, 2021) and the disordered regions may also affect the properties of the folded domains (Yu and Sukenik, 34 2023). For example, there is a complex interplay between the folded and disordered regions in the RNA-binding 35 protein hnRNPA1, that affects its conformational ensemble in solution and its propensity to undergo phase sep- 36 aration (Martin et al., 2021b). However, describing the conformational ensembles of MDPs in solution generally 37 requires a combination of biophysical experiments and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations (Thomasen and 38 Lindorff-Larsen, 2022). 39 All-atom MD simulations have been used to generate conformational ensembles of IDPs and MDPs and 40 to study intra- and inter-domain interactions (Zheng et al., 2020; Sekiyama et al., 2022). Such simulations, 41 however, are often limited by the large system sizes and long time scales which limit efficient sampling of 42 these dynamic proteins. Coarse-grained (CG) models may increase the sampling efficiency by reducing the 43 number of particles in the simulation systems (Neri et al., 2005; Monticelli et al., 2008; Bereau and Deserno, 44 2009; Gopal et al., 2010). The accuracy, transferability, and efficiency of such models, however, depend on 45 the degree of coarse-graining and the parameterization strategy (Heo and Feig, 2023). One commonly used 46 model is the Martini force field, which uses a four-to-one mapping scheme with explicit solvent (Souza et al., 47 2021). Different versions of Martini have been modified to produce improved ensembles of IDPs and MDPs 48 (Benayad et al., 2020; Thomasen et al., 2022, 2023). For IDPs, there has in the last years been extensive work 49 using even coarser models where each amino acid residue is represented by a single bead. The interaction sites 50 are generally located at the C훼position and separated by bonds that are 0.38 nm long, and we therefore here 51 term these C훼models. Several related models rely on a similar functional form to the HPS model introduced by 52 Dignon et al. (2018) and may include bonded terms, an Ashbaugh-Hatch potential (Ashbaugh and Hatch, 2008) 53 for shorter-range interactions and a Debye-Hückel electrostatic screening potential. Such models have for 54 example been used to study the conformational ensembles and interactions within and between IDPs (Dignon 55 et al., 2018; Joseph et al., 2021; Regy et al., 2021; Dannenhoffer-Lafage and Best, 2021; Wessén et al., 2022; 56 Tesei and Lindorff-Larsen, 2023; Valdes-Garcia et al., 2023). 57 Coarse-grained models developed for IDPs do not represent the stability of folded proteins well, because the 58 finely balanced energy contributions from individual backbone and side-chain interactions are not captured by 59 the reduced representation. As a consequence, additional (often harmonic) restraints are applied to maintain 60 the folded configurations in folded proteins and MDPs (Souza et al., 2021; Borges-Araújo et al., 2023). Even 61 when applying such restraints to models developed for IDPs, extra attention needs to be paid to interactions 62 related to folded domains since it is still unclear whether the models are fully transferable to MDPs. In particular, 63 C훼-based one-bead-per-residue mappings do not account for the specific orientations of side chains in folded 64 proteins. For example, hydrophobic residues, whose side chains are ‘tucked away’ in the hydrophobic core of 65 the protein, may be exposed at the surface of the protein in a C훼based representation. One approach to help 66 overcome this problem is to use a different or scaled set of force field parameters for interactions that involve 67 folded regions (Kim and Hummer, 2008; Dignon et al., 2018; Krainer et al., 2021). Another possible solution is 68 the introduction of more terms in the energy function to better describe long-range interactions (Li et al., 2012; 69 Tan et al., 2023) or to introduce anisotropic interactions (Sieradzan et al., 2022). 70 As an alternative, other coarse-grained models represent a residue by more than one bead to represent 71 backbone side chain orientations and interactions (Pappu et al., 1996; Hyeon et al., 2006; Maity et al., 2022; 72 Zhang et al., 2022; Sieradzan et al., 2022; Mugnai et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Yamada et al., 2023). In some 73 of these models, one bead is placed at C훼and the other one is at the centre of mass (COM) of side chain atoms. 74 In this way, side chain interactions can be explicitly taken into account, improving the simulated dynamical 75 behaviour of folded protein simulations and model transferability. In previous studies, this strategy has been 76 used to study conformational ensembles of IDPs or unfolding pathways of proteins (Hyeon et al., 2006; Mugnai 77 et al., 2023). While effective, using multi-bead-per-residue models increases the time to sample configurations 78 in simulations, and requires the determination of a larger number of force field parameters. 79 We have previously developed and applied an automated procedure to optimize the ‘stickiness’ param- 80 eters (휆) in a one-bead-per-residue model by improving the agreement with experimental small-angle X-ray 81 scattering (SAXS) and paramagnetic relaxation enhancement (PRE) NMR data for a large set of IDPs (Norgaard 82 et al., 2008; Tesei et al., 2021b; Tesei and Lindorff-Larsen, 2023). The most recent CALVADOS (Coarse-graining 83 Approach to Liquid-liquid phase separation Via an Automated Data-driven Optimisation Scheme) model (CAL- 84 VADOS 2) was further tuned to describe phase behaviour of multi-chain conformational ensembles of IDPs 85 from simulations by reducing the range of non-ionic interactions (Tesei and Lindorff-Larsen, 2023). 86 Here, we explore the use of the CALVADOS model for simulations of MDPs. We find that when the CAL- 87 VADOS 2 parameters are used in simulations of MDPs with interaction sites at the C훼positions, the resulting 88 structures in some cases show excessive interactions between the folded domains, leading to compact en- 89 sembles that do not agree with SAXS data. To remedy this problem, we describe a strategy where interaction 90 sites in folded regions are located at the COM of the residue, and show that simulations with this model result 91 in substantially improved agreement with experiments. We optimize the parameters in CALVADOS using the 92 COM representation to derive a refined set of CALVADOS parameters (CALVADOS 3). When we combine the 93 COM representation of folded domains with harmonic restraints between residues in the folded domains and 94 the CALVADOS 3 parameters we obtain good agreement with experimental data on single-chain properties of 95 MDPs and IDPs. Finally, we show how this model may be used to study the interactions between folded and 96 disordered regions in proteins that undergo phase separation. 97

We term this combination of the force 104 field parameters (CALVADOS 2) and the C훼representation of the interaction sites in the folded domains as 105 CALVADOS2C훼. In particular, we found that the 푅푔was underestimated for 109 several MDPs including a series of two fluorescent proteins connected by Gly-Ser linkers of different lengths 110 (GS-proteins; Moses et al. (2024)). This observation was confirmed by calculations of the relative mean signed 111 deviation, rMSD, between experimental and calculated values of 푅푔that shows that these are on average un- 112 derestimated by 18% in the MDPs (Figure 1A). 113 We hypothesized that the compaction of several MDPs was a result of placing the interaction sites at the C훼 114 positions in the folded domains. In particular for 훽-sheet-containing proteins, this geometry would mean that 115 residues whose side chains are buried inside the folded domain are represented by interaction sites located 116 closer to the protein surface (Figure 1A); thus buried hydrophobic residues might appear as solvent exposed. 117 We therefore constructed a new model where the interaction sites within folded regions were placed at the 118 COM of the residue (Figure 1B) and constrained by harmonic restraints; when used with the CALVADOS 2 pa- 119 rameters, we term this model CALVADOS2COM. In the absence of folded domains, CALVADOS2COM 122 and CALVADOS2C훼are thus identical and simulations with the two models gave comparable results (Figure 1A 123 and B). In addition to the COM 126 representation, we also examined whether a side-chain centre-of-mass (SCCOM) representation, shifting bead 127 positions of buried residues further away from the surface, could yield even more accurate 푅푔predictions than 128 the COM representation (Figure 1C). We performed single chain simulations with the CALVADOS 2 parameters 129 and the SCCOM representation (CALVADOS2SCCOM) and found that CALVADOS2SCCOM on average resulted in 130 an overestimation of the 푅푔of MDPs of 11% (Figure 1B and C). Therefore, we proceeded by exploring the COM 131 representation in this study. 132 To examine in more detail why the CALVADOS2C훼model resulted in more compact conformations of MDPs 133 than CALVADOS2COM, we calculated the time-averaged non-ionic (Ashbaugh-Hatch) interaction energies be- 134 tween residues of different folded domains. For this analysis we selected GS0, a construct with two fluorescent 135 proteins separated by a 29-residue-long linker (Moses et al., 2024), since the 푅푔value of GS0 deviates substan- 136 tially from experiments in simulations with CALVADOS2C훼(Figure 1A). In the energy maps, we see evidence of 137 substantial inter-domain interactions between residue 140–230 of one fluorescent protein and residue 340– 138 440 of the other (Figure 2A). The comparison of the two energy maps thus supports the hypothesis 140 that the too compact conformations of MDPs in simulations with CALVADOS2C훼result from inter-domain at- 141 tractions that are decreased in the COM representation (Figure 2C). 142

Optimizing CALVADOS using a centre-of-mass representation 143 Having shown that the COM representation gave an improved description of MDPs while preserving the ac- 144 curacy when simulating IDPs, we proceeded to optimize the CALVADOS model further. We used our iterative 145 Bayesian optimization scheme (Norgaard et al., 2008; Tesei et al., 2021b) to optimize the 휆stickiness parame- 146 ters of the CALVADOS model targeting simultaneously SAXS and NMR data on 56 IDPs and 14 MDPs (Table S1, 147 Table S2, Table S3). In these simulations we used the COM representation of the folded domains and we thus 148 term the final model CALVADOS3COM to represent both the force field and the COM representation of the 149 folded regions. The resulting 휆values in CALVADOS3COM are similar to those in CALVADOS 2 (Figure 3 and Fig- 150 ure S1). We found that simulations of IDPs with CALVADOS3COM and CALVADOS2COM gave similar agreement 151 to SAXS experiments. Likewise, we find a similar agreement for the MDPs (Figure 1B, Figure 3B and C). 152 Having optimized 휆, we validated the CALVADOS3COM model on 25 IDPs and 9 MDPs (Table S4, Table S5) 153 that were not used in training for any of the models (Figure 4). For the 25 IDPs we found good agreement for 154 all three models (CALVADOS2C훼CALVADOS2COM and CALVADOS3COM) with CALVADOS3COM performing com- 155 parably (Figure 4A–C). (Since the COM representation is only applied to the folded domains, these are all C훼 156 representations and for IDPs CALVADOS2C훼CALVADOS2COM are therefore the same models). In contrast, for 157 MDPs we found that CALVADOS3COM and CALVADOS2COM perform substantially better than CALVADOS2C훼 158 (Figure 4A-C). Our validation results thus show that the CALVADOS3COM model gives improved agreement for 159 simulations of MDPs while retaining the accuracy for IDPs with CALVADOS2C훼. Across the 34 independent 160 test proteins we find ⟨휒2

푅푔⟩values of 49, 22 and 15 for CALVADOS2C훼, CALVADOS2COM and CALVADOS3COM, 161 respectively (Figure 4D), and both CALVADOS2COM and CALVADOS3COM have essentially no bias (rMSD≈0; Fig- 162 ure 4B,C). 163

Simulations of phase separation of disordered and multi-domain proteins 164 We and others have previously used one-bead-per-residue models such as CALVADOS to study the self-association 165 and phase separation of IDPs (Dignon et al., 2018; Tesei et al., 2021b; Joseph et al., 2021; Regy et al., 2021; 166 Dannenhoffer-Lafage and Best, 2021; Wessén et al., 2022; Tesei and Lindorff-Larsen, 2023; Valdes-Garcia et al., 167 2023). In some cases, these models have also been used to study phase separation of proteins that contain 168 a mixture of folded and disordered regions (Dignon et al., 2018; Conicella et al., 2020; Her et al., 2022). We 169 therefore examined whether the CALVADOS3COM model could be used to study phase separation of both IDPs 170 and MDPs. We used multi-chain simulations in a slab geometry (Dignon et al., 2018) to simulate the partitioning 171 of proteins between a dilute and dense phase, and calculated the dilute phase concentration (the saturation 172 concentration; 푐sat) as a sensitive measure of the accuracy of the model. We first simulated 32 IDPs and found 173 that simulations with CALVADOS3COM gave an agreement with experimental values of 푐sat that is comparable 174 to that of CALVADOS2C훼(Table S6, Figure S2, Figure S3). 175 We then proceeded to use CALVADOS3COM to study the phase separation of MDPs including hnRNPA1* 176 (where * denotes that residues 259–264 have been deleted from full-length hnRNPA1), full-length FUS (FL_FUS) 177 and other multi-domain proteins with experimental estimates of 푐sat (Table S7; Wang et al. (2018); Martin et al. 178 (2021b)). Simulations of hnRNPA1* with CALVADOS2C훼, under conditions where the experimental dilute phase 179 concentration is 0.17 mM, resulted in essentially all proteins in the dense phase (푐sat=0 mM; Figure 5A). In 180 contrast, simulations using CALVADOS3COM resulted in a lower propensity to phase separate and a calculated 181 value of 푐sat=0.18±0.02 mM that is closer to experiments (Figure 5B). To understand the origin of these differ- 182 ences we calculated an interaction energy map of the proteins in the dense phase. Experiments have shown 183 that the LCD in hnRNPA1* (residues 186–320) plays a central role in driving phase separation (Molliex et al., 184 2015; Martin et al., 2021b), and we indeed found evidence for substantial LCD-LCD interactions in the dense 185 phases in simulations with both CALVADOS2C훼(Figure 5C) and CALVADOS3COM (Figure 5D). In the simulations 186 with CALVADOS2C훼we, however, also observed more substantial interactions between the folded RRM (RNA 187 recognition motif) domains (residues 14–97 and 105–185) and between the RRMs and the LCD. In simulations 188 with CALVADOS3COM these interactions were much weaker, presumably explaining the increase of 푐sat in these 189 simulations. 190 Having demonstrated that CALVADOS3COM provides a more accurate description of the phase behaviour 191 of hnRNPA1* than CALVADOS2C훼, we proceeded to perform simulations of several other MDPs for which we 192 found estimates of 푐sat in the literature (Figure 6, Figure S4). As for hnRNPA1*, we found that CALVADOS2C훼 193 substantially overestimates the tendency of these proteins to undergo phase separation (i.e. underestimate 194 푐sat). The use of the COM representation in CALVADOS3COM decreases the protein-protein interactions, and 195 thus substantially improves the agreement with experiments, though differences remain. 196

Discussion 197 In this work, we found that simulations with the CALVADOS2C훼model, previously shown to represent single- 198 chain and multi-chain properties of IDPs, underestimated the radius of gyration of MDPs. Changing the CG 199 mapping method from C훼to COM substantially improved the agreement with experimental data. The resulting CALVADOS3COM model provides a good description of both single- and multi- 202 chain simulations of both IDPs and MDPs. 203 The relatively low 푐sat value calculated from slab simulations of hnRNPA1* with CALVADOS2C훼further sup- 204 ported that interactions between the folded domains are overestimated by C훼-based models without any fur- 205 ther modifications. Considering that the SCCOM-based model (CALVADOS2SCCOM) overestimated 푅푔of MDPs, 206 we suggest that the COM-based model (CALVADOS3COM) appears to strike a good balance, leading to improved 207 values of 푐sat for MDPs. Nevertheless, some systematic differences remain even with this model, which resulted 208 in underestimates of 푐sat for different constructs of the protein FUS. A summary of the training data and other 209 properties of the CALVADOS models is shown in the supplement (Table S8). Together, our results show that 210 the new parameter set and the centre-of-mass representation (CALVADOS3COM) retain the accuracy of CALVA- 211 DOS 2 for IDPs, but improve the description of proteins with both disordered and folded domains. We there- 212 fore term this new model CALVADOS 3, with the implicit notion that this model is used with centre-of-mass 213 representation of residues within folded regions. 214 When simulating MDPs with CALVADOS 3 we need to restrain the folded domains using harmonic restraints. 215 In the current work we have manually determined the boundaries for which regions are considered to be folded, 216 though automated methods will be needed for large-scale applications. Tools for automatic predictions of 217 domain boundaries exist (Holm and Sander, 1994; Lau et al., 2023) and might be combined with AlphaFold to 218 set the harmonic restraints (Jussupow and Kaila, 2023). 219 Despite these current limitations, we envision that the CALVADOS 3 model will enable detailed studies of 220 the interactions within and between multi-domain proteins, and pave the way for proteome-wide simulation 221 studies of full-length proteins similar to what has recently been achieved for IDRs (Tesei et al., 2023). 222

Methods 223 Description of the model 224 We modelled each amino acid by one bead. We generated C훼-beads for IDPs and assigned C훼atom coordinates 225 to bead positions for IDRs in multi-domain proteins according to their modelled or experimental structures (see 226 below). For structured domains, we used the following rules for the different representations: we placed each 227 bead position at the C훼atom (C훼representation), or the centre of mass calculated for all the atoms in a residue 228 (COM representation), or the centre of mass calculated for only side chain atoms of residues (SCCOM represen- 229 tation). Simulations 269 We generated initial conformations of all IDPs as Archimedes’ spirals with a distance of 0.38 nm between bonded 270 beads. Atomistic structures of all MDPs used in optimization procedures, single-chain validation and slab sim- 271 ulations either came from our recent work (Thomasen et al., 2023) or were modelled by superposing experi- 272 mental domain structures (if available) on AlphaFold predictions (Jumper et al., 2021; Varadi et al., 2022). We 273 then mapped all of these MDPs to CG structures based on different CG representations (C훼, COM, SCCOM). 274 We conducted Langevin dynamics simulations using OpenMM 7.6.0 (Eastman et al., 2017) in the NVT en- 275 semble with an integration time step of 10 fs and friction coefficient of 0.01 ps−1. Single chains of 푁residues 276 were simulated in a cubic box with a (푁−1)×0.38 + 4 nm box edge length under periodic boundary conditions. 277 Each chain was simulated in 20 replicas for 6.3∼77.7 ns depending on the sequence length of the disordered 278 regions (Tesei and Lindorff-Larsen, 2023; Tesei et al., 2023). Final trajectories had 4000 frames for each protein, 279 excluding the initial 10 frames in each replica. 280 We performed direct-coexistence simulations in a cuboidal box using [퐿푥, 퐿푦, 퐿푧] = [17, 17, 300] and [15, 15, 150] nm 281 to simulate multi-chains of Ddx4WT and the other IDPs, respectively. We generated each IDP chain as an Archimedes spiral with 284 a distance of 0.38 nm between bonded beads in the xy-plane. Each spiral was placed along the z-axis with 285 a 1.47 nm interval. Before production simulations, we performed 288 equilibrium runs where we used an external force to push each chain towards the centre of the box so that 289 a condensate could be formed. We then continued to perform production simulations, saving frames every 290 0.125 ns and discarded the first 0.15 μs before analysis.
